intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that brachyolmia type 4 with mild epiphyseal and metaphyseal changes (BCYM4) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the PAPSS2 gene (also called ATPSK2) on chromosome 10q23-q24.

paragraphs.text: Brachyolmia type 4 with mild epiphyseal and metaphyseal changes is an autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasia that mainly affects the spine. Affected individuals have short-trunk short stature with normal intelligence and facies. Radiographic features include rectangular or flattened vertebral bodies with irregular endplates and narrow intervertebral discs. Involvement of the epiphyses and metaphyses of the tubular bones is mild and variable (Ahmad et al., 1998; Miyake et al., 2012). Miyake et al. (2012) concluded that PAPSS2 mutations cause a family of skeletal dysplasias, with phenotypes ranging from brachyolmia to spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia (SEMD). Noordam et al. (2009) found PAPSS2 deficiency in a girl with premature pubarche and androgen excess.

paragraphs.text: Ahmad et al. (1998) described a large inbred kindred from a remote area of Pakistan, spanning 8 generations, with a distinct form of spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia. They evaluated 16 affected individuals (11 males and 5 females). Clinical findings included short stature evident at birth, short bowed lower limbs, mild brachydactyly, kyphoscoliosis, an abnormal gait, enlarged knee joints, precocious osteoarthropathy, and normal intelligence. Radiographs showed delayed epiphyseal ossification at the hips and knees and platyspondyly with irregular end plates. They also showed narrowed joint spaces and diffuse early osteoarthritic changes, mainly in the spine and hands. Mild metaphyseal abnormalities were seen, mostly at the hips and knees. The authors considered the phenotype distinct from other autosomal recessive forms of SEMD because metaphyseal involvement was mild, because of the type of brachydactyly, and because loose joints and other clinical findings were absent.

paragraphs.text: Miyake et al. (2012) studied 3 affected members of a Turkish family with autosomal recessive brachyolmia, plus 3 other patients with a similar phenotype (2 Japanese and 1 Korean). All 6 patients had short-trunk short stature that became conspicuous during childhood, with normal intelligence and facies. Radiographic features included rectangular vertebral bodies with irregular endplates and narrow intervertebral discs. Other features were precocious calcification of the rib cartilages, short femoral neck, and mildly shortened metacarpals. The spinal changes were very similar in all 6 patients, but epiphyseal and metaphyseal changes of the tubular bones varied.

The sulfotransferase SULT2A1 converts DHEA to its inactive sulfate ester, DHEAS, and needs 3-prime-phosphoadenosine-5-prime-phosphosulfate (PAPS) to do so. The authors concluded that PAPSS2 deficiency is a monogenic adrenocortical cause of androgen excess.

paragraphs.text: Miyake et al. (2012) used exon capture and next-generation sequencing in 3 affected members of a Turkish family with autosomal recessive brachyolmia. They found a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the PAPSS2 gene (c.337_338insG; p.A113GfsX18). The authors then studied 3 more patients with similar brachyolmia phenotypes (2 Japanese and 1 Korean) and found loss-of-function mutations in PAPSS2 in each of them. One patient was homozygous for IVS3+2delT. The second was compound heterozygous for c.616-634del19 (p.V206SfsX9) and c.1309-1310delAG (p.R437GfsX19). The third was compound heterozygous for c.480_481insCGTA (p.K161RfsX6) and c.661delA (p.I221SfsX40).

paragraphs.text: Miyake et al. (2012) studied 3 patients of Japanese or Korean origin with brachyolmia. One of them was compound heterozygous for 2 mutations in the PAPSS2 gene. The first was a 4-bp insertion (c.480_481insCGTA) causing a frameshift (p.K161RfsX6). The second was a 1-bp deletion (c.661delA; p.I221SfsX40). The authors described both as loss-of-function mutations.
